food.title: Wagassi
food.intro: Soft, fresh and gently salted, wagassi is the cheese of Fulani pastoral life—and an edible path into the landscapes of northern Benin.
food.heading: A landscape,
food.p1: Wagassi begins with fresh milk and the leaves of the calotropis plant, whose sap gently separates curds from whey. The method travels through families—measured less by recipe than by touch, sound and attention.
food.p2: In markets across Benin you will see ivory rounds stacked neatly, sometimes stained rust-red with sorghum leaves. Grilled over charcoal or simmered in sauce, it becomes a bridge between pastoral north and coastal table.
food.makerHeading: Aïssatou knows when milk is ready by the way it moves.
food.makerBody: Near Parakou, Aïssatou Bio turns the morning’s milk into wagassi as her mother taught her. Visit her small cooperative, taste the cheese warm, and understand why patience is its first ingredient.
related: The women who carry wagassi south

experience.title: Cotonou after dark
experience.intro: Follow the smoke, the music and the evening crowd on a food walk through the city’s most generous street kitchens.
experience.whyHeading: Come hungry. Leave knowing the city better.
experience.whyP1: Street food is Cotonou in miniature: fast-moving, deeply social and full of exacting opinions. With local cook Rosine, start with hot talé-talé, cross town for grilled wagassi, and finish over peppered fish near the lagoon.
experience.whyP2: This isn’t a tasting checklist. Rosine introduces the people behind each fire and explains the ingredients, migrations and daily rituals held in every plate.

story.title: Rosine cooks without recipes.
story.dek: At Dantokpa, one cook turns the morning market into a map of memory, instinct and extraordinary flavor.
story.heroAlt: Rosine and a fellow cook at their market stall
story.p1: By six in the morning, Rosine has already tasted the pepper twice. She does not measure it. She watches how the sauce holds to the back of her wooden spoon, adds a little salt, then turns to greet a customer she knows by voice.
story.p2: Her stall sits where the market begins to fold into the street. Plantains are stacked at one edge. A charcoal fire occupies the other. Between them, in a space no wider than her outstretched arms, Rosine makes breakfast for half a neighborhood.
story.quote: A recipe cannot tell you what the tomato did in the rain.
story.imgAlt: A market cook preparing the morning meal
story.imgCaption: Morning preparation at the edge of Dantokpa
story.p3: Rosine learned beside her aunt, first washing bowls, later tending the fire. What she remembers is not a list of ingredients but a sequence of gestures: the weight of a ripe tomato, the sound oil makes when it is ready, the exact moment to lower the flame.
story.p4: “You have to listen,” she says. “Food always says what it needs.”
story.endBody: Join her evening food walk through Zongo and Ganhi.

food.title: What will you
food.lede: Dishes, markets and makers—the country, first, at the table.
food.p1: Food is how most people first feel at home in Benin: not through a single restaurant, but through dawn markets, evening grills, and the quiet confidence of a shared plate.
food.p2: This section gathers the tastes that open the country: cheese from the north, red rice of the coast, fritters between errands, and buying with someone who knows the stalls.

experience.title: What will you
experience.lede: Time spent with people who already hold the place—on water, at market, on a path of memory.
experience.p1: An experience here is not a product checklist. It is a clear invitation: a first table, a crossing, a night that follows the smoke, a walk taken with care.
experience.p2: Five meals for your first days, a crossing of Ganvié, a careful walk in Ouidah, a night that follows the smoke in Cotonou.

story.title: What will you
story.lede: Field notes, portraits and guides—angles into a living country.
story.p1: Stories are how BA holds complexity: a cook without recipes, a market before heat, a park that asks for planning, a faith approached without caricature.
story.p2: Read slowly. These are not tips to collect—they are angles into a living country.

place.title: Where will you
place.lede: Cities on water, markets that set the clock, roads that change colour before they change speed.
place.p1: Bonne Assise maps Benin through places that still hold their own rhythm—not as a checklist of stops, but as rooms you enter with attention.
place.p2: Start south where the lagoon organises life, or further inland where history sits close to the surface. Leave room for the north when you have days to spare.
